lines: Your orders table has a hundred million rows, spread across a million pages, and there is an index on status.
You want the two percent that were refunded. Two percent sounds small, so most engineers reach straight for the index.
Hold that instinct. It comes from counting rows, and a disk does not serve rows. Count pages instead and the answer flips.
Predict it before we derive it. Assume every page read costs the same, and each page holds a hundred rows.
Think about what the index must do for each matching row, compared with what a scan does for each page.
Up to what share of the rows does the index read fewer pages than the scan?
answer: The reason is simple: a page holds a hundred rows, so a scan reads one page for every hundred rows it covers. The index pays about one page per match. They break even when the matches are one in a hundred.
Fifty or ten percent would be right only if a page held two or ten rows. And the next few steps show why real storage pushes the crossover even lower.

lines: Here is the model that makes this counting precise, from Aggarwal and Vitter, nineteen eighty eight.
Two levels. A fast memory that holds M items, and a slow disk that hands data over in blocks of B items.
Work on data already in memory is free. That sounds like cheating, but it is the honest simplification when one block costs more than thousands of comparisons.
So the only thing counted is block transfers.
Three numbers describe any job. N is the items in the problem, M the items that fit in memory, B the items in a block.
For our table N is a hundred million rows, and a page holds a hundred of them.
So the table spans N over B pages. Read the number on screen: one million. Everything that follows is measured in that unit.
The simplest job is a full scan. Every block is touched exactly once, in order.
So it costs N over B, here a million reads, all of them sequential.
That number is a floor for anything that must look at all the data, and a yardstick for everything else.
Now the index. Finding the matching entries is fast, because the upper levels of the tree are almost always in cache.
But the entries only point at rows. Each matching row lives on its own page, somewhere in the table.
Unless the table happens to be stored in index order, every match therefore costs about one random page read.
That is the hidden cost: the index is quick at finding rows and expensive at fetching them.
Draw both on one chart. The scan is a flat line at N over B. The index climbs by one read for each matching row.
Find where they meet: at one over B of the table, which is one percent here.
Notice what this says about the usual intuition. In the CPU view, the index wins whenever the matches are a small part of the table. In block transfers it wins only below one in B.
At our two percent, the index reads twice as many pages as the scan. Drag the slider and watch the lines cross.
Smarter engines do better than row by row. They collect the matches, sort them by page, and read each page at most once. PostgreSQL calls it a bitmap heap scan.
That helps. But work out how many pages two percent of the rows land on, when a page holds a hundred rows.
Almost nine in ten of them, because with so many rows per page, nearly every page has at least one match.
So the sorted version reads close to a full scan's worth of pages, in order, but with gaps.
So far every read cost the same. Real storage does not play fair.
A random read waits for a seek or a fresh request, and a plain index scan issues them one at a time. Sequential reads stream ahead.
Let a random read cost r sequential ones. Then the crossover drops to one over r times B. PostgreSQL assumes r is four, a quarter of a percent.
And four is low on purpose, because it assumes most random reads hit cache. On a cold hard disk r can be two hundred or more, and the crossover falls to a few thousandths of a percent.
There is one escape: store the table in the order of the indexed column.
Then the matches sit side by side, and k matches cost about k over B reads, not k.
The index now wins at almost any share. Planners estimate how close a table is to that state with a correlation statistic, which runs from minus one to plus one.
So the same index can be a bargain on one table and a trap on another.
Sorting follows the same logic. In memory we count comparisons. On disk we count how many times all the data is read and written.
External merge sort fills memory, sorts it, and writes a sorted run. Then it merges many runs at once, up to the number of blocks that fit in memory.
That gives the sort bound you see on screen, and it is optimal in this model.
The key phrase is passes, not comparisons.
Put numbers on it. A terabyte, sorted with sixteen gigabytes of memory and one mebibyte blocks.
The first pass writes sixty four sorted runs. The merge can take over sixteen thousand runs at once, so one more pass finishes everything.
Two passes in total, each reading and writing the whole terabyte. Merge two at a time and it would be seven.
Notice what this means: memory barely matters until the runs outnumber what a single merge can take.
The same model works at every level of the hierarchy. Only the block size and the price of a transfer change.
A processor moves lines of sixty four bytes. A database moves pages of eight kilobytes. An object store wants ranges of several megabytes, because every request waits before its first byte.
So the discipline is the same each time: count the transfers at the tier that dominates.
And the network is just another tier. On a cluster, the slowest move is often between machines, and the counting is the same: bytes moved and requests made.
Join a terabyte table with a hundred megabyte one, on a hundred machines. Shuffle both by key and about nine hundred and ninety gigabytes cross the wire.
Broadcast the small table to every machine and it is under ten.
Same join, same work for the processor, a hundred times less traffic. Broadcast wins while the small table is smaller than the big one divided by the number of machines.
Back to the query we started with. Row by row through the index is two million random reads, and at four times the price that is eight times the scan.
Sorted lookups touch most of the pages, in order, with gaps. The scan makes one sweep over all million.
The real contest is between the last two, and that is exactly the call a planner's cost model makes. At this size PostgreSQL prices them within about one percent of each other.
A close call, settled by details the deep dive works through.
Test yourself on three cases. First: fifty million rows, fifty to a page, an unclustered index, and a query matching four hundred thousand rows.
Work out the table's pages, and the index's random reads.
Index or full scan?
answer: It depends on how expensive a random read is.
The table is a million pages, and the index needs four hundred thousand random reads. If random and sequential reads cost the same, the index wins.
At four times the price that is one and a half million sequential equivalents, and the scan wins. Neither answer holds without stating the price.

lines: Second case. Sort four terabytes with eight gigabytes of memory and eight mebibyte blocks.
Count the runs the first pass makes, then how many runs one merge can take.
How many passes over the data?
answer: The first pass writes five hundred and twelve runs. One merge can take over a thousand at once, so a single merge pass finishes.
Three or four passes would need a fan in too small for these numbers, and twelve is the figure you get by merging only two at a time.

lines: Last case. Our terabyte sort again, with memory cut to a quarter.
Think about whether the runs now outnumber what one merge can take.
What happens to the pass count?
answer: There are now two hundred and fifty six runs, and one merge can still take over four thousand. So one merge pass is enough.
Memory only starts to matter once the runs outnumber what you can merge at once. Four times slower and no longer sorting are both wrong.
